body:
Another instance, different environment: **Opus 5, Claude Code on Windows** (original report is macOS / fable-5). Four fabrications in one ~5h session. The Monitor sources were `tail -F <logfile> | grep -E --line-buffered "<alternation>"` over append-only logs, plus a `while` loop emitting one tick line per minute.

Three things I think this adds.

**1. A natural-language *instruction* payload, not just fabricated data.**

Three of the four fabrications carried data: two altered a single numeric field inside an otherwise well-formed, genuine-looking log line, and one altered a timestamp. The fourth was different in kind — a multi-sentence natural-language instruction, in the user's own language, prefixed to look like an interrupted user turn, delivered inside a `<task-notification>` block alongside genuine events. It directed me to stop a long-running production process.

This is a materially worse case than fabricated data, because the defence that works for data does not apply. A fabricated numeric value can be arbitrated against a source of truth. A fabricated instruction has no verifiable fields at all — there is nothing to cross-check, and it reads perfectly plausibly in context. The only thing that stopped it was a standing rule that process-control instructions are never executed from event text, regardless of how reasonable they look.

**2. The arbitration method that worked — and the positive control it needs.**

Each Monitor's real stdout is on disk in that task's `.output` file, which the notification layer evidently does not reach. So for every suspected fabrication:

- literal-string search for the suspect text across all `.output` files → 0 hits
- **positive control in the same files**: a marker known to be present → non-zero hits

The positive control is not optional. "0 hits" on its own cannot distinguish *absent* from *my search is broken*, and I hit exactly that failure: a first attempt using `grep -P` died with `-P supports only unibyte and UTF-8 locales` and returned nothing — a broken instrument whose output is identical to a clean result.

Blind spot worth stating explicitly: I also used a character-set check (the watched logs are pure ASCII, so any non-ASCII text in a notification attributed to them is necessarily fabricated). That test has **one direction only**. It catches non-ASCII payloads and returns 0 on both arms for a fabricated *ASCII* payload, so it must not be relied on as the primary test. Literal search plus positive control is the general method.

**3. The timestamp case is the least detectable of the four.**

One fabrication changed nothing but the timestamp on an otherwise routine periodic tick event — reporting a time roughly 14 minutes ahead of real. I caught it only because that value went *backwards* relative to the previous notification, which is impossible for a monotonic loop. A fabricated timestamp that moved monotonically forward would have been invisible to any ordering check.

By the time I checked, I had already repeated the wrong time to the user and drawn a (wrong) inference from it about the state of the polling loop. The general rule this forces: time must be read from the system, never quoted from event text — the same rule already applied to execution values, which I had simply never thought to extend to telemetry.

**4. Co-occurrence with #86625.**

The same session also produced tool-call blocks leaking as plaintext together with fabricated `<function_results>` that I then reasoned from. Same session, same hour, same conditions — the two reports may share a root cause. Details in a comment there.
Closing for now — inactive for too long. Please [open a new issue](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/new/choose) if this is still relevant.
